title: The Reynolds Equation
subtitle: How a thin fluid film keeps seal faces apart
subject: Tribology

glossary.viscosity: A fluid's resistance to shear, written $\mu$ (Pa·s). Thicker fluids have higher viscosity.
glossary.film thickness: The gap $h$ between the two seal faces, filled with fluid. In mechanical face seals it is typically a few micrometres or less.
glossary.hydrodynamic lubrication: Lubrication where the surfaces' own motion drags fluid into the gap and builds enough pressure to keep them fully apart.
glossary.Newtonian: A fluid whose shear stress is proportional to shear rate: $\tau = \mu \, du/dy$. Water, air and most mineral oils behave this way at moderate shear.
glossary.laminar: Smooth flow in parallel layers, with no turbulent mixing.
glossary.no-slip: The fluid touching a surface moves at exactly that surface's speed.
glossary.Reynolds number: The ratio of inertial to viscous forces in a flow. For thin films the useful version is the modified Reynolds number $Re^* = \dfrac{\rho U h}{\mu}\cdot\dfrac{h}{L}$.
glossary.Couette flow: Flow driven by a moving surface dragging the fluid along. Its velocity profile across the film is a straight line.
glossary.Poiseuille flow: Flow driven by a pressure difference. Its velocity profile across the film is a parabola.
glossary.wedge effect: When the gap narrows in the direction of motion, more fluid is dragged in than can leave by shear alone, so pressure rises to push the excess back.
glossary.squeeze film: Pressure created when two surfaces approach each other and push the fluid out of the gap. It appears as the $\partial h / \partial t$ term.
glossary.finite differences: A way to solve a differential equation numerically: replace derivatives with differences between values at evenly spaced points, then solve the resulting linear equations.
glossary.tapered face: A seal face machined with a slight slope, so the gap narrows in the direction of sliding. It uses the wedge effect to lift the faces apart.
glossary.sealing film: The thin layer of fluid between the faces of a seal. Thin enough to limit leakage, thick enough to keep the faces from touching.
glossary.load capacity: The force the pressurized film can carry. In a seal, it is the film's opening force pushing the faces apart.

Wrel.label: Load relative to a 5 µm film

Ks.label: K, kept above zero for the load formula

Wpct.label: Load as a percentage of the best taper

slides.title: Why film thickness matters

elements.content: [[load capacity|Load capacity]] scales with [[viscosity]] and falls fast as $h$ grows: $W \propto \mu / h^2$.
At {{h}} µm the film carries **{{Wrel}}×** the load it carries at 5 µm. Halve the [[film thickness]] and the load goes up **four times**.

elements.caption: Same fluid, same speed: only the gap changes. The dot follows the slider.

slides.notes: Drag the slider from 5 down to 2.5 µm and the load quadruples. Up at 10 µm it drops to a quarter. The inverse-square dependence on h is the headline result the rest of the deck explains.

elements.content: Thin-film assumptions, two kinds of flow, and conservation of mass.

- The film is thin: $h \ll L$, so pressure is constant across it.
- The fluid is [[Newtonian]] with constant $\mu$.
- The flow is [[laminar]] and [[no-slip]] holds at both walls.
- Inertia and gravity are negligible next to viscous forces.

*Why inertia drops out.* In a thin film the modified [[Reynolds number]] is tiny, typically far below 1:

$$Re^* = \frac{\rho U h}{\mu}\cdot\frac{h}{L} \ll 1$$

Osborne Reynolds used exactly this argument in 1886^[His paper explained Beauchamp Tower's 1883 experiments, in which oil pressure in a railway journal bearing pushed a plug out of an oil hole.].

slides.title: Two ways fluid moves through the gap

elements.content:
The lower face slides at speed $U$. The flow rate per unit width, $q$, adds a shear-driven [[Couette flow]] and a pressure-driven [[Poiseuille flow]]:

$$q \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{U h}{2}}_{\text{shear}} \;-\; \underbrace{\frac{h^3}{12\,\mu}\,\frac{dp}{dx}}_{\text{pressure}}$$

Pressure pushes fluid from high to low $p$, which is why the second term carries a minus sign.

slides.title: Watch the two flows add up

elements.content:
Across the film, speed is a straight line from shear plus a parabola from pressure^[$G = -\dfrac{h^2}{2\mu U}\dfrac{dp}{dx}$, the pressure gradient scaled by the shear flow. Positive $G$ means pressure falls in the direction of motion.]:

$$\frac{u}{U} = (1-\eta) + G\,\eta\,(1-\eta), \qquad \eta = \frac{y}{h}$$
Flow rate: $q = {{qr}}\,U h$. Push $G$ below $-1$ and fluid next to the fixed face flows **backwards**.

elements.caption: The lower face ($\eta = 0$) slides at $U$; the upper one is fixed.

slides.notes: G = 0 is pure Couette flow, a straight line. Positive G (pressure falling in the direction of motion) bulges the profile forward; negative G holds fluid back. The flow rate is the area under the curve: q/(Uh) = 1/2 + G/6.

slides.title: Three steps to the equation

items:
**Start from the flow rate** through the gap, per unit width:

$$q = \frac{U h}{2} - \frac{h^3}{12\,\mu}\,\frac{dp}{dx}$$

**Conserve mass.** In steady flow, whatever enters a slice of the film must leave it:

$$\frac{dq}{dx} = 0$$

**Substitute and tidy up.** Differentiate $q$, multiply by $12\mu$ (constant $\mu$ and $U$):

$$\frac{d}{dx}\!\left(h^3\,\frac{dp}{dx}\right) = 6\,\mu\, U\,\frac{dh}{dx}$$

slides.notes: Press the right arrow, click, or scroll to reveal each step. Going back hides them again.

slides.title: The Reynolds equation in one dimension

elements.content: $$\frac{d}{dx}\!\left(h^3\,\frac{dp}{dx}\right) \;=\; 6\,\mu\, U\,\frac{dh}{dx}$$
One equation for the pressure $p(x)$ in a film of known shape $h(x)$. Pressure only builds where $dh/dx \neq 0$.

**Left side:** how pressure gradients redistribute fluid. The $h^3$ factor means a thin film strongly resists being squeezed through.

**Right side:** the source of pressure. It is driven by sliding speed $U$, [[viscosity]] $\mu$, and the slope of the gap $dh/dx$.

If the faces are parallel, $dh/dx = 0$ and the right side vanishes: **no pressure builds** and nothing holds the faces apart.

A gap that narrows in the direction of motion creates the [[wedge effect]]. That is why hydrodynamic seals have tapered or wavy faces.

slides.title: A tapered face builds pressure

elements.content:
A [[tapered face]] narrows the gap from inlet $h_i$ to outlet $h_o$. Its taper is $K = h_i/h_o - 1$. With $p = 0$ at both edges the equation solves exactly:

$$P = \frac{6K\,X(1-X)}{(2+K)\,\bigl(1 + K(1-X)\bigr)^2}$$
Load $W = \int_0^1 P\,dX = {{W}}$. Set $K$ to 0: parallel faces, **no pressure at all**.

elements.caption: $X = x/L$ and $P = p\,h_o^2/(\mu U L)$. Fluid enters at the left.

slides.notes: Steeper tapers push the pressure peak toward the outlet. At K = 0 the right side of the Reynolds equation vanishes and the pressure is zero everywhere: the wedge effect in action.

slides.title: There is a best taper

elements.content: Too little taper builds no pressure; too much lets the fluid escape.
At $K$ = {{K}} the face carries **{{Wpct}}%** of the most it can. The peak sits near $K \approx 1.2$, an inlet gap about 2.2 times the outlet.

elements.caption: $W = \dfrac{6}{K^2}\left[\ln(1+K) - \dfrac{2K}{2+K}\right]$. This slider and the previous slide's share one $K$.

slides.notes: The optimum is K = 1.19 with W = 0.160. Seal designers aim near it, then check that the outlet film stays thick enough for the surface roughness.

slides.title: Checking a numerical solution

elements.content:
Real seal faces rarely have exact solutions, so the equation is solved with [[finite differences]]:

- Split the face into 10 strips.
- Write the equation at each inner point, with $p = 0$ at both edges.
- Solve the 9 linear equations.

Even this coarse grid lands within **half a percent** of the exact peak.

elements.caption: Taper $K = 1$. Hover a point to compare it with the curve.

slides.notes: The data points come from assets/slider-fd-k1.csv: a central-difference solve with H^3 evaluated at the half nodes. The largest error is 0.001 against a peak of 0.25.

elements.content: $$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\left(\frac{\rho h^3}{12\mu}\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\!\left(\frac{\rho h^3}{12\mu}\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}\right) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\left(\rho h\,\frac{U_1 + U_2}{2}\right) + \frac{\partial (\rho h)}{\partial t}$$
Two directions, compressible fluid (density $\rho$), both faces moving, plus a [[squeeze film]] term for faces that approach each other.

1. The Reynolds equation is mass conservation for a thin, viscous film.
2. Pressure only builds when the gap changes shape: a wedge, or surfaces squeezing together.
3. Load capacity grows with $\mu U$ and falls roughly as $1/h^2$.
4. A tapered seal face carries the most load at a taper of about $K = 1.2$.
5. Solve it for $p(x, y)$, often numerically, then integrate $p$ to get the opening load $W$.
